cards.front: What makes ticketing different from other inventory
cards.back: Every unit is unique: seat F7 at the 7 pm show is one specific thing exactly one person may own.

cards.front: Booking rate for 1M bookings a day
cards.back: About 12 a second on average. Tiny for one database, except when everyone targets the same show.

cards.front: The real job in a hot release of 1M people for 50k seats
cards.back: 95% leave without tickets, so tell them quickly and fairly rather than trying to serve them all.
A hold gets every requested seat or none, so a family is never split across a row they didn't choose.
A bitmap of 2 bits per seat (free, held, sold) is 50 bytes in Redis. Layout is static and cached forever by layout_version.

cards.front: Why a slightly stale seat map is fine
cards.back: A seat that looks free but was just taken costs one 'pick another' from the hold call, far cheaper than having 100k viewers a second read the source of truth.

cards.front: Three ways to place a hold
cards.back: Row lock (never across a payment page), conditional update with expires_at, or Redis SET NX EX per seat in a Lua script.

cards.front: The last line of defence against double booking
cards.back: UNIQUE (show_id, seat_id) on booked seats. If holds ever leak, the second insert fails and that payment is refunded.
Seats on hold = holds started per minute × minutes each hold lasts.

cards.front: What happens to a payment that arrives after the hold expired
cards.back: If someone else booked the seat the insert fails; mark the booking EXPIRED and refund. Extending holds during in-flight payments makes it rare.
Everyone arriving before opening gets a random place in line; after that, first come first served.
Inventory is table slots for a seating length; a Postgres exclusion constraint rejects overlapping reservations. No-shows, not bots, are the risk.

quiz.q: Holds use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and keep the lock while the user is on the payment page. What goes wrong at a busy show?
choices: Locks pile up while users dither, blocking other buyers
quiz.why: Never keep a database lock open across a payment page.

quiz.q: A Redis failover lets two users hold seat F7 and both pay. What prevents a double sale?
choices: UNIQUE (show_id, seat_id): the second insert fails and is refunded
quiz.why: The database unique key has the final say.

quiz.q: During a release the show looks sold out, but later hundreds of seats come back. What is happening?
choices: The unique key is rejecting bookings
Holds from abandoners lock seats until they expire; shorter holds help
The CDN is serving the wrong layout
quiz.why: Little's law: holds per minute × minutes held is the number of seats hidden.

quiz.q: One blockbuster show's bookings are slowing down bookings for all other shows. What design fixes this?
choices: Shard holds and bookings by show_id and give blockbusters their own capacity
quiz.why: Partitioning by show isolates hot shows from the other 250k.

quiz.q: The payment provider times out for a booking with an active hold. What should the service do?
choices: Keep the hold, query the provider, and let reconciliation check stuck bookings
Charge again with a new key
quiz.why: A timeout is not a failure; resolve before deciding.

quiz.q: All 50,000 seats are sold or held and 600,000 people are still in the waiting room. What should it do?
choices: Say 'sold out, join the waitlist' without admitting anyone further
Keep admitting at the same rate
Admit everyone so they can see the seat map
quiz.why: The sold-out fast path tells people quickly.

quiz.q: Stadium buyers keep fighting over the same seats and holds fail repeatedly. What reduces contention?
choices: Best available: users pick a tier and quantity and the server picks adjacent seats
quiz.why: Server-chosen seats mean holds succeed on the first try.
